To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the sellers practice price discriminating across market segments, (ii) the more asymmetric the equilibria, the higher the expected volume of transactions and transaction price, and (iii) the more asymmetric equilibria lead to a lower expected utility of the buyers, a higher expected profit of the sellers, and, therefore, a higher probability of successful collusion.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of advertising in a market where the buyers are heterogeneous in the sense that they are contacted by sellers with different probabilities.
the effects of market segmentation on the distribution of prices and on the expected profits of the sellers.
the effects of market structure and market segmentation on the sellers’ equilibrium strategies, and the buyers’ expected utility.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sellers’ profits are maximized when the market is segmented in a way that is consistent with the sellers’ ability to discriminate among buyers.
a seller who can reach a buyer more easily than another seller will be able to charge a lower price.

, in general, the sellers’ profits are increasing in the degree of price discrimination and that, in general and in the long run, the degree of price differentiation increases with the degree of market segmentation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sellers’ ability to discriminate among buyers and the buyers’ ability to identify the sellers who discriminate more are important determinants of the equilibrium.
a model of advertising can be used to study price discrimination and collusion.
, in a market with a continuum of buyers with homogeneous preferences, price discrimination can be a powerful tool to sustain collusion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sellers can increase their expected profits by influencing the distribution of buyers across segments, which in turn affects the distribution of transaction prices.
the sellers' expected profits are higher when they practice price discrimination across buyers.
, even when buyers have homogeneous preferences, the sellers can practice price discrimination and collude to increase their expected profits.
